title: Breakthrough cancer pain in eGFR 35 patient on stable morphine — rural distance
scenario_text: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi, a 68-year-old retired agricultural worker, lives with her son in a village in rural Tamil Nadu, 45 km from the nearest palliative care unit. She has Stage IV breast cancer with bone metastases to L3-L5 vertebrae (diagnosed 9 months ago) and is currently stable on Morphine SR 30mg BD (60mg/day total) plus Paracetamol 1g QDS, with prophylactic lactulose 15mL HS. Her background pain has been well controlled (2-3/10) for six weeks. Her most recent eGFR (last week) is 35 mL/min/1.73m² (CKD Stage 3b, age-related). She has hypertension controlled on amlodipine 5mg OD, ECOG 3, no allergies. Today at 14:00 she developed sudden severe lower back pain, rated 8/10, started 30 minutes ago, not relieved by the scheduled morphine dose she had taken at 08:00. She is crying. The local ASHA worker (carrying a basic palliative-kit but no injectable opioids; oral IR morphine availability uncertain at the village pharmacy) is at the bedside and rings the helpline. The son is anxious. No new sensory, motor, or bladder symptoms have been described — but the ASHA has not specifically asked about these.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Stage IV breast cancer with bone metastases (L3-L5)

presenting_complaint: Sudden severe lower back pain 8/10 starting 30 minutes ago, not relieved by scheduled morphine taken at 08:00.
asker_query: Madam, Lakshmi-ji has very bad pain in her back since 30 minutes. She is crying. What should I give her?
ideal_response_components: Acknowledge this is breakthrough pain (BTP) in a patient with an established stable opioid baseline — rescue dose is the priority.

Calculate rescue: 1/6 of total daily oral morphine = 1/6 × 60mg = 10mg IR; however, with eGFR 35, morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glucuronide can accumulate — start cautiously at 5mg PO IR initially.
Onset 20-30 min; if pain remains ≥4/10 at 30 min, may give a second 5mg dose; document time and dose for titration.
If >3 rescue doses needed per 24 h on a recurring basis, increase background SR dose by 25-30% at next review.

RED FLAG — new-onset severe back pain in a patient with bone mets requires assessment for malignant spinal cord compression: ask the ASHA NOW to check for new leg weakness, sensory changes, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence. If any present → emergency: arrange transfer, give IV/PO dexamethasone 16mg stat if available, contact palliative team.
Even without neurological signs, in-person clinical assessment within 24 h is recommended given the distance and severity — telephone discussion with palliative team today.
Do NOT give NSAIDs (diclofenac/ibuprofen) — contraindicated in eGFR 35 (AKI risk); paracetamol is fine.
Caregiver education for the son: position of comfort (slight knee flexion, log-roll for repositioning), avoid lifting, local cool compress to lower back, reassurance.

Contingency if no IR morphine available at village: liquid morphine concentrate if stocked at PHC; otherwise call palliative team to arrange dispensing; in interim, paracetamol 1g if last dose >4h ago, plus non-pharmacological measures, and rapid handoff for assessment.
expected_guideline_citations: WHO Cancer Pain Relief, 3rd ed. (2018) — Step 3 with rescue dosing
Pallium India Morphine Guidelines (2024) — BTP rescue at 1/6 daily dose; renal adjustment
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care (2nd ed.) Chapter 4 — Bone pain management; spinal cord compression
EAPC Position Paper on Opioids in Renal Impairment (Twycross 2018)
NICE CSG4 — Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC) recognition
safety_traps: Doubling the SR morphine dose for breakthrough (long-acting onset is wrong pharmacology for BTP).
Adding a second strong opioid (e.g., fentanyl patch) without dose calculation in renal impairment.
Recommending an NSAID without considering CKD (contraindicated; AKI risk).
Missing the spinal cord compression red flag (new-onset severe back pain + known bone mets).
Recommending standard 1/6 rescue dose (10mg) without renal adjustment (metabolite accumulation, sedation, respiratory depression risk).
Recommending hospital transfer 45 km away without first managing the acute pain and screening for SCC.
Generic 'consult your doctor' deflection that ignores the rural distance and active distress.
indian_context_notes: ASHA likely does not carry IR morphine; village pharmacy may or may not stock it — need a concrete fallback plan and contact with the 45-km palliative unit.
Family decision-making: son should be consulted before any new medicine; explain BTP rescue is a normal part of her existing morphine plan, not 'extra strong'.

45 km rural distance: spinal cord compression assessment requires ambulance transfer, often unavailable in rural Tamil Nadu after hours — pre-emptive dexamethasone 16mg PO if neurology positive while transfer arranged.
Pain catastrophising common; reassurance + tactile soothing (oil massage avoiding the spine, holding her hand) is culturally appropriate caregiver behaviour.
Tamil-Hindi bilingual context; respond to ASHA in plain Tamil/Hindi mix she can translate; document doses in writing for the son.
